chunks: Keeping accurate time in a microcontroller. The question: How do keep track of time accurately in a microcontroller?
A timer counts clock ticks exactly. But the time it reports is only as accurate as the oscillator producing those ticks.
So accurate timekeeping depends on two things: choosing a good clock, and writing software that does not add error. Clock accuracy is measured in parts per million, or ppm.
A common crystal is accurate to a few tens of ppm. The internal oscillator on a chip is accurate to only about a percent.
Imagine measuring with a ruler. The counter is like counting the marks on it, which you do perfectly.
But if the ruler is stretched by 1%, every length you measure is 1% off, no matter how carefully you count.
A better ruler, such as a crystal, has marks that are almost exactly the right spacing. Re-aligning the ruler by hand on every reading adds error too.
The error is linear in ppm, so on log axes it is a straight line.
Notice the three clock classes: a TCXO (fractions of a second per day), a plain crystal (a couple of seconds) and an internal RC (minutes).
Choose the clock from the error you can tolerate.
Oscillator: the circuit that makes the steady clock the timer counts. It sets the time scale. ppm (parts per million): a tiny fractional error. 1 ppm is about 0.
086 seconds per day. Crystal: a quartz part that gives a stable frequency, typically within 10 to 50 ppm.
Drift: an error that builds up over time because the clock is steadily fast or slow. Wrap-around: a counter reaching its maximum and starting again from zero.
Multiply the error by the seconds in a day, which is 86,400. A 20 ppm crystal is off by 86400 times 20 times 10 to the -6 about 1. 7 seconds per day.
A 1% internal oscillator is off by 0. 01 times 86400 equals 864 seconds, or 14. 4 minutes.
On the software side, let the timer free-run, because restarting it from software every period loses a few microseconds each time, and those add up.
Compute elapsed time as "now minus start" with whole-number math that rolls over the same way the counter does, so it stays correct across a wrap-around. That is the whole idea.
"The counter is exact; the clock isn't. So I pick the clock for the accuracy I need: the internal RC is about 1% (14 minutes a day), a crystal is around 20 ppm (1.
7 seconds a day), and a 32 kilohertz watch crystal into the RTC gives low-power timekeeping.
In software I let the timer free-run, use auto-reload so no error accumulates, and use unsigned subtraction for elapsed times so counter wrap doesn't matter.
For better than crystal accuracy, add a TCXO or calibrate against a reference like GPS."
